name: Association fallacy
statement: An idea is judged by the company it keeps, and naming the rival party's leader as a bill's backer moved opinion against the bill while its text stayed the same.
meaning: Two claims sit inside the name. The descriptive one is that people carry valence across from a thing to whatever stands beside it. The normative one is that doing so is an error. Guilt by association is the negative form and honour by association the positive one. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's fallacy list files guilt by association under ad hominem, defining it as holding a person guilty of error because of the group they associate with. It files the genetic fallacy separately, as discrediting a claim because of its origin. The difference is where the damaging information sits. A genetic argument looks backwards, to where a claim came from. An association argument looks sideways, to who else holds it or what it sits next to. Leo Strauss's reductio ad Hitlerum is the sideways form aimed at a view rather than at a person. The horn effect, entry 175, follows the same spread between traits of a single person. This entry is about spread between a claim and its company.

origin.note: Strauss names the move on pages 42 and 43, where he writes that the examination must avoid 'the fallacy that in the last decades has frequently been used as a substitute for the reductio ad absurdum: the reductio ad Hitlerum. A view is not refuted by the fact that it happens to have been shared by Hitler.' He presents it as already common rather than as something he has discovered, and he attaches no name to whoever used it first. The passage was read in the scanned text of the 1953 edition at the Internet Archive. Guilt by association is older than the phrase and older than Strauss, and where either name was coined could not be established here.

evidence: The closest test of the fallacy proper is Harris, Hsu and Madsen, who put the ad Hitlerum into three experiments and asked whether the shift it produces tracks how diagnostic the association is. In the first, 61 volunteers read five dialogues in which one speaker argues that a proposal is bad because Hitler did it or liked it, then rated how convinced the listener should now be. The same argument form was rated as differently convincing across the five topics, F(3.43, 240) = 16.74, p < .001, partial eta squared .22. Participants then estimated how many good and how many bad German policies of 1925 to 1945 Hitler was responsible for. A Bayesian prediction built from those estimates, with no free parameters, correlated with mean posterior ratings at radj(3) = .94, p < .05. The mean within-participant correlation was .24. Experiment 2 gave 184 people the likelihood figures explicitly through a third speaker, setting them at .8 and .2 or the reverse. Ratings moved with the manipulation, F(1, 178) = 56.50, p < .001, partial eta squared .24, and the prediction tracked the condition means at radj(4) = .95, p < .01. Religion was the one topic whose error bars did not overlap the prediction. Experiment 3 replaced Hitler with Zhang, a fictional ruler of Planet Xenon, and gave 725 people explicit frequencies across 17 conditions crossed with argument direction. Ratings followed the frequencies, F(16, 691) = 5.96, p < .001, partial eta squared .12, correlating with objective predictions at r(18) = .88 and with predictions from participants' own likelihoods at r(18) = .92. Direction also mattered on its own, F(1, 691) = 79.86, p < .001, partial eta squared .10, an effect the Bayesian predictions did not contain. Nicholson took the same structure into real politics. Using 2008 Cooperative Congressional Election Study samples, he held two bills' text and the endorsed position fixed and varied only whose name was attached. Among Democrats, opposition to a foreclosure bill rose from 11 percent with no cue to 28 percent when John McCain was named, z = -2.93, p < .05. Democratic support for an immigration bill fell from 52 percent to 33 percent under the same cue, z = 2.22, p < .05. Among Republicans, opposition to that immigration bill rose from 66 percent to nearly 90 percent when Barack Obama was named, a 24 point gap, z = -3.09, p < .05. In-party cues did nothing significant in any of the four comparisons. The person mattered more than the party label: a McCain cue raised Democratic opposition to the foreclosure bill 20 points above a Republican Party cue, z = 3.21, p < .05. Cohen's four studies report the ingroup half of the same picture. Their abstract concludes that attitudes towards a social policy depended almost exclusively upon the stated position of the participant's party. Participants denied having been influenced, and expected others to be. The laboratory literature on transfer by pairing is evaluative conditioning, which measures liking rather than belief. Staats and Staats ran the first controlled version in 1958, pairing nationality words with positive or negative words and finding the paired nationalities rated accordingly. Hofmann, De Houwer, Perugini, Baeyens and Crombez pooled 214 studies and report a mean effect of d = .52, 95 percent confidence interval .466 to .582. About 70 percent of the variance in effect sizes was attributable to systematic variation. Moran, Krava and Shilat pooled the applied end of it in 2025, 505 effect sizes from 23,845 participants across 115 studies. They got Hedges's g = 0.21, with some evidence of publication bias, and call the procedure minimally efficient as a way of changing attitudes and behaviour. Applied work on people rather than claims runs under stigma by association. Pryor, Reeder and Monroe report across three studies that companions of stigmatised people are devalued, and that when the relationship looks coincidental rather than meaningful only implicit attitudes moderate the devaluation. Hebl and Mannix report that a male job applicant was rated more negatively when seen with an overweight woman than with a woman of normal weight. Mere proximity was enough. The effect held regardless of the apparent depth of the relationship, the rater's anti-fat attitudes or gender.

replication.headline: The association effect holds in artificial materials and shrinks sharply in realistic ones, and the claim that pairing works without the person noticing failed a twelve-lab preregistered test.
replication.detail: The formal replication on record concerns the unaware version of evaluative conditioning. Moran and 25 colleagues across twelve labs ran a preregistered close replication of Olson and Fazio's surveillance task with 1,478 participants. Under the original authors' own awareness exclusion rule, dropping 9.2 percent of the sample, the effect survived at Hedges's g = 0.12, 95 percent confidence interval 0.05 to 0.20, z = 3.17, p = .002, against g = 0.27 in the original and g = 0.20 in the authors' meta-analysis of the published literature. Under the three stricter awareness rules the effect disappeared: g = 0.05, interval -0.04 to 0.13; g = 0.03, interval -0.06 to 0.13; and g = 0.05, interval -0.03 to 0.13. Between-site heterogeneity was zero in all four models. Participants scored as aware showed effects of g = 0.24 to 0.37, and under three of the four rules the aware and unaware groups differed reliably. The authors put observed power in the original at .13 and median power in the published surveillance-task literature at .14. On the fallacy proper the disagreement is about size rather than direction. Skytte took 70 real news articles about political proposals, prepared each with and without the party cues that occur naturally in the coverage, and ran them past representative American samples totalling 12,177 people, reporting mostly modest effects on policy opinion. Dür and Mateo ran survey experiments in several countries on the proposed Transatlantic Trade and Investment Partnership and the 2015 Paris Agreement, and report that the arguments interest groups make matter more than the groups named as their source, holding after adjusting for trust in the group and for how much the respondent knew. Bullock's two experiments report that when people hold any information about a policy their attitudes are affected at least as much by that information as by cues from party elites. So the effect is real, and it is largest where the material is thin.

study.cite: Moran, T., Hughes, S., Hussey, I., Vadillo, M. A., Olson, M. A., Aust, F., et al. (2021). Incidental Attitude Formation via the Surveillance Task: A Preregistered Replication of the Olson and Fazio (2001) Study. Psychological Science, 32(1), 120-131. Twelve labs, N = 1,478.

limits: Evaluative conditioning measures liking, not belief. Its dependent variable is how pleasant a nonword or a face is rated, and nothing in that literature shows that a claim is judged less likely to be true because of what it was paired with. Reading it as a test of the fallacy replaces the question. Association is also sometimes diagnostic, and Harris and colleagues built their experiments on exactly that point: the same argument form was rated as very different in force depending on the topic, and its force tracked the participants' own conditional probabilities. Dowden's fallacy list makes the parallel remark about origins, that appeals to them are sometimes relevant and sometimes not, and that borderline cases are hard to call. Coverage of the sources here is uneven. The Hofmann meta-analysis is closed access; its article was not opened, and the pooled d and its interval are quoted from the abstract as published at PubMed. Cohen, Pryor and colleagues, Hebl and Mannix, Skytte, Dür and Mateo, and Bullock were likewise read at their abstracts, at PubMed for the first three and at Crossref for the rest. No figure from any of them appears above beyond what those abstracts state. Nicholson's cells are small, running from about 50 to 90 respondents in the tables comparing party with candidate cues, and his significance tests are one-tailed unless stated otherwise. His design also holds the endorsed position constant across parties, which is not how endorsements arrive in life. Searches for a meta-analysis of stigma-by-association effects were run against Crossref bibliographic records and PubMed titles and abstracts on 17 August 2026. They returned meta-analyses of weight stigma and of cultural variation in mental-illness stigma, and none pooling the spread of stigma to companions.
misreadings: The commonest error is to offer evaluative conditioning as proof of the fallacy. It shows that pairing shifts liking, which is a different dependent variable from belief in a claim. Its strong version, that the shift happens without the pairing being noticed, is the part that failed the twelve-lab test. The second error is treating every appeal to a claim's company as fallacious. People do not apply it uniformly, and Harris and colleagues found the shift tracked the diagnosticity of the association closely enough that a model with no free parameters predicted the condition means. Where Hitler's endorsement carried little information the argument moved almost nobody, and where it carried a lot it moved people a long way. The third error confuses this with the genetic fallacy. Dowden's list keeps them apart, putting guilt by association under ad hominem and reserving the genetic fallacy for arguments about where a claim originated. Strauss himself described the reductio ad Hitlerum as a substitute for the reductio ad absurdum, not as an argument about origins. The fourth reads Nicholson's result as showing that endorsements persuade. His in-party cues produced no significant movement in any of the four comparisons. What moved people was the rival's name, and the rival's name moved them further than the rival's party label. Strauss is also miscredited with coining the practice as well as the phrase. He wrote that the move had frequently been used in the preceding decades.

sources.text: Harris, A. J. L., Hsu, A. S., & Madsen, J. K. (2012). Because Hitler did it! Quantitative tests of Bayesian argumentation using ad hominem. Thinking & Reasoning, 18(3), 311-343. Author manuscript read in full; every statistic attributed to it here was re-checked against the extracted text.

Nicholson, S. P. (2012). Polarizing Cues. American Journal of Political Science, 56(1), 52-66. Read in full from the copy on the author's university page. The source for the cue percentages, the null in-party results and the candidate-versus-party comparison.

Moran, T., Hughes, S., Hussey, I., Vadillo, M. A., Olson, M. A., Aust, F., et al. (2021). Incidental Attitude Formation via the Surveillance Task: A Preregistered Replication of the Olson and Fazio (2001) Study. Psychological Science, 32(1), 120-131. Accepted manuscript read in full at the Ghent University repository, where it carries the title 'A Registered Replication Report'. Data and preregistration at osf.io/z2vts.

Moran, T., Nudler, Y., & Bar-Anan, Y. (2023). Evaluative Conditioning: Past, Present, and Future. Annual Review of Psychology, 74, 85-114. Read in full as the authors' preprint. The source for Staats and Staats, for the shift in what awareness studies conclude, and for the statement that recent reviews find no robust evidence for unaware encoding.

Hofmann, W., De Houwer, J., Perugini, M., Baeyens, F., & Crombez, G. (2010). Evaluative conditioning in humans: a meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 136(3), 390-421. Closed access and not opened; the 214 studies, the mean d of .52 and its interval are quoted from the abstract as published at PubMed, PMID 20438144.

Moran, T., Krava, L., & Shilat, Y. (2025). Evaluative conditioning interventions: A systematic review and meta-analysis focused on attitudinal and behavioral change outcomes. Psychological Bulletin, 151(8), 1061-1088. Read at its PubMed abstract, PMID 41100277, which is the source for the 505 effect sizes, the 23,845 participants and Hedges's g of 0.21.

Pryor, J. B., Reeder, G. D., & Monroe, A. E. (2012). The infection of bad company: Stigma by association. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 102(2), 224-241. Read at its PubMed abstract, PMID 22082057. Not obtained in full, and no figure from it appears above.

Hebl, M. R., & Mannix, L. M. (2003). The weight of obesity in evaluating others: a mere proximity effect. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 29(1), 28-38. Read at its PubMed abstract, PMID 15272957. Not obtained in full.

Skytte, R. (2025). The effect of real-news party cues. American Journal of Political Science, 70, 1196-1212. Abstract read at Crossref, which is the source for the 70 articles, the 12,177 participants and the description of the effects as mostly modest.
Dür, A., & Mateo, G. (2019). How interest groups influence public opinion: Arguments matter more than the sources. European Journal of Political Research, 58(2), 514-535. Abstract read at Crossref.
Bullock, J. G. (2011). Elite Influence on Public Opinion in an Informed Electorate. American Political Science Review, 105(3), 496-515. Abstract read at Crossref.

Cohen, G. L. (2003). Party over policy: The dominating impact of group influence on political beliefs. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 85(5), 808-822. Read at its PubMed abstract, PMID 14599246, which is the source for the wording quoted above.

Strauss, L. (1953). Natural Right and History. University of Chicago Press, pages 42-43. Scanned text read at the Internet Archive and searched for 'Hitlerum'; the quoted sentences are as they appear there.

Dowden, B. Fallacies. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. The definitions of guilt by association, of ad hominem circumstantial and of the genetic fallacy, and the remark that appeals to origins are sometimes relevant. A search of the page text for 'association fallacy' returned only guilt by association.
